feedback: Written before this robot has raced. Iteration 2 (5 sensors at y=0.07 m, 16 mm, track 0.10 m, radius 0.035 m, mass 0.6 kg) is the best design so far: score 329, oval finish rate 65%, oval mean finish 1.80 s, 7 of 20 oval runs off track. Iteration 3 (7 sensors at y=0.08 m) lowered the oval finish rate to 35% and raised steering_oscillation from about 0.28 to 0.36 on the oval, so extra look-ahead and spread did not help as a package. Iteration 1 showed that spread alone did not cut line losses. The Integrator has kept the controller unchanged from Iteration 2, so this geometry's effect on speed is isolated. Depending on the next race: if the oval finish rate rises above 65% with off-track exits falling, the speed limit is the bottleneck, so raise wheel_radius further to 0.045 m. If the oval finish rate rises but off-track exits also rise with max_error near 0.043 m, the speed is outrunning steering, so reduce mass to 0.5 kg or widen wheel_track to 0.11 m rather than adding speed. If steering_oscillation stays near 0.28 and the finish rate does not move, the geometry is not the bottleneck and the next change should be the controller, not the sensors.
requested_changes: If the oval finish rate rises above 65% with fewer off-track exits, raise wheel_radius from 0.040 to 0.045 m. Iteration 2 showed the oval finish time has about 1.2 s of margin, so more ground speed is the cheapest route to more finished runs.

If off-track exits rise on the oval while max_error stays near 0.043 m, reduce mass from 0.6 to 0.5 kg with wheel_radius 0.040 m. Iteration 3 showed that extra steering load (more sensors and higher oscillation) lowered finish rate, so reducing inertia should help the same bends at higher speed.

If steering_oscillation stays near 0.28 and the finish rate does not move, keep the Iteration 2 sensor layout (5 sensors, y=0.07 m, 16 mm) and widen wheel_track from 0.10 to 0.11 m for yaw stability. Iterations 1 and 3 showed that changing the sensor layout alone did not improve the finish rate.
